34250: Carmel's caves (Nahal Me'arot) preserve some of the longest records of prehistoric human occupation, now a UNESCO site.
34253: The northernmost city of Israel at a source of the Jordan, captured by the tribe of Dan. Jeroboam I set up one of his golden calves here, and "from Dan to Beersheba" described the whole land.
34254: Avraham Biran's excavations found the Tel Dan Stele (1993-1994), an Aramaic victory inscription naming a king of Israel and the "house of David", the earliest extra-biblical reference to David's dynasty. Also preserved are a Middle Bronze mudbrick arched gate and a large Iron Age cultic platform.
34256: An early capital of the northern kingdom from Jeroboam's or Baasha's time until Omri moved the court to Samaria. Zimri burned the palace over himself here after a reign of seven days.
34257: Roland de Vaux's excavations at Tell el-Far'ah found an Iron Age town with an unfinished building phase that some connect with Omri's move to Samaria.
34261: A Phoenician coastal town between Tyre and Sidon where a widow fed Elijah during the drought and he raised her son. Jesus cited her as a foreigner to whom the prophet was sent.
34262: James Pritchard's excavations (1969-1974) uncovered potters' kilns, a shrine with an inscription to Tanit-Ashtart, and industrial quarters of the Phoenician town.
34264: The name Deuteronomy and the prophets use for the mountain of the covenant, generally taken as another name for Sinai. Moses met God in the burning bush here, and Elijah fled here and heard the still small voice. Its location is debated along with Sinai's; the point shown is Jebel Musa.
34267: An oasis city at the foot of the Anti-Lebanon and capital of the Aramean kingdom that fought Israel for a century. Naaman preferred its rivers to the Jordan. Saul was converted on the road to Damascus and later escaped the city in a basket.
34268: Continuous occupation limits excavation, but the Street Called Straight (Via Recta) still runs east-west through the old city, and the Umayyad Mosque stands over a Roman temple of Jupiter and a church of John the Baptist.
34271: The leading Phoenician port, built partly on an island. King Hiram supplied cedar and craftsmen for David and Solomon; Ezekiel prophesied its ruin; Jesus visited its region, and Paul found disciples there.
34272: Alexander the Great took the island city in 332 BC by building a causeway, which silted into the present isthmus. Visible remains include a Roman hippodrome, colonnaded road and necropolis.
34275: An ancient Phoenician port whose name often stands for all Phoenicians. Jezebel was the daughter of a Sidonian king. Jesus said Tyre and Sidon would have repented at his works, and Paul visited friends here on his voyage to Rome.
34276: Finds include the temple of Eshmun nearby and royal sarcophagi such as the Alexander Sarcophagus and the inscribed sarcophagus of King Eshmunazar II.
34278: The great Assyrian capital on the Tigris under Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal. Jonah was sent to preach there and the city repented; Nahum celebrated its fall to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.
34279: Layard's excavations uncovered Sennacherib's "palace without rival" with the Lachish reliefs, and Ashurbanipal's library of clay tablets including the Gilgamesh flood story. Sennacherib's prism describes shutting up Hezekiah in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage".
34281: The empire centred on the upper Tigris (Assur, Nimrud, Nineveh) that dominated the Near East in the 9th to 7th centuries BC. It made Israel and Judah vassals, destroyed Samaria in 722 BC and deported its people, and besieged Jerusalem under Sennacherib in 701 BC.
34282: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (Nimrud, 841 BC) shows Jehu or his envoy bowing; royal annals name Ahab, Menahem, Hoshea and Hezekiah.
34284: Capital of Nebuchadnezzar's empire on the Euphrates, which destroyed Jerusalem and took Judah into exile. Cyrus of Persia took it in 539 BC. In the New Testament "Babylon" becomes a cipher for Rome and the world's opposition to God.
34285: Koldewey's excavations (1899-1917) uncovered the Ishtar Gate and Processional Way (now in Berlin). Ration tablets list Jehoiachin, king of Judah, as a captive, and the Cyrus Cylinder describes Cyrus restoring deported peoples and their gods.
34288: The old Elamite capital that became a winter royal residence of the Persian kings. The book of Esther is set in its citadel, Nehemiah served Artaxerxes here, and Daniel saw a vision by the Ulai canal near Susa.
34289: French excavations uncovered the palace and great audience hall (apadana) of Darius I with glazed-brick friezes of archers. The stele bearing Hammurabi's law code was found at Susa in 1901, carried there as plunder.
34292: The ceremonial capital founded by Darius I and expanded by Xerxes (Ahasuerus), the Persian kings who appear in Ezra and Esther. It is not named in the Bible but shows the court world behind the return from exile.
34293: The Apadana reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing tribute. Thousands of administrative tablets record rations and workers. Alexander burned the palaces in 330 BC.
34295: A distant western source of silver, iron, tin and lead, reached by "ships of Tarshish"; Jonah tried to flee there. The most common identification is Tartessos in southwestern Spain; alternatives include Sardinia, Carthage and Tarsus, and some read "ships of Tarshish" simply as a class of large seagoing ships.
34298: The ancient port of the central coast where cedar for the temple was landed and where Jonah took ship for Tarshish. Peter raised Tabitha here and, on the roof of Simon the tanner's house, received the vision preparing him to visit Cornelius.
34299: Excavations have uncovered a Ramesside Egyptian gate (13th century BC) and successive Iron Age, Hellenistic and Roman levels.
34301: A Levitical town of Benjamin a few kilometres northeast of Jerusalem, where Solomon banished the priest Abiathar. It was Jeremiah's home; its men plotted against him, and during the siege he bought a field there as a sign that land would again be bought in Judah. Usually placed at Ras el-Kharrubeh near the village of Anata.
34304: A town on the edge of the Judean wilderness south of Bethlehem. Joab brought a wise woman from Tekoa to persuade David, and the prophet Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa.
34307: An irrigation canal near Nippur in Babylonia beside which Judean exiles, including Ezekiel at Tel-abib, were settled. Ezekiel saw his vision of God's throne-chariot there.
34308: Business documents of the Murashu family from Nippur (5th century BC) mention the naru kabari ("great canal") and many Judean names. The Al-Yahudu tablets show a "town of Judah" of exiles in the same region.
34311: Judah's second city, guarding the Shephelah. Sennacherib besieged and took it in 701 BC while threatening Jerusalem, and in Jeremiah's time it was one of the last cities to hold out against Babylon.
34312: Sennacherib's palace reliefs from Nineveh (British Museum) depict the siege in detail; the Assyrian siege ramp and Judean counter-ramp survive. The Lachish Letters (ostraca found 1935) record an officer's messages as Babylon closed in, mentioning that the signal fires of Azekah could no longer be seen.
34314: The hometown implied by Elijah's title "the Tishbite", in Gilead east of the Jordan. It is usually placed at el-Istib (Listib) in northern Jordan, near a Byzantine church of Mar Elias, but some read the Hebrew as "of the settlers of Gilead" rather than a town name.
34316: Elisha's hometown in the Jordan valley, where Elijah found him ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen. Proposed sites include Tel Abu Sus west of the Jordan (shown) and Tell el-Maqlub or other sites east of the river.
34317: The incense-trading kingdom of the Sabaeans in southwest Arabia (Yemen), with its capital at Marib. Its queen visited Solomon to test his wisdom. Ethiopian tradition, set out in the Kebra Nagast, instead places her realm in Ethiopia.
34318: Marib has a great dam (from the 8th century BC or earlier) and the temple of Almaqah (Mahram Bilqis). Sabaean inscriptions document a kingdom of trade in frankincense and myrrh.
34321: The river running from the slopes of Hermon through the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea, the eastern border of the promised land. Israel crossed it on dry ground under Joshua, Elijah and Elisha parted it, Naaman was healed in it, and John baptised Jesus in it.
34326: The salt lake at the lowest point on earth's land surface, fed by the Jordan and without outlet. Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the temple to make its waters fresh and full of fish.
34327: The Dead Sea Scrolls were found from 1947 in caves near Qumran on its northwest shore, including the Great Isaiah Scroll, a millennium older than previously known Hebrew manuscripts.
34332: A freshwater lake about 21 km long, the centre of Jesus' Galilean ministry. Fishermen including Peter, Andrew, James and John were called from its shore; Jesus calmed a storm and walked on its water, and the risen Jesus met disciples beside it.
34333: A 1st-century fishing boat (the Galilee Boat) was recovered from the mud near Ginosar in 1986. Harbours have been traced around the shore at Capernaum, Magdala and elsewhere.
34336: A small Galilean village in the hills above the Jezreel valley, home of Mary and Joseph, where Jesus grew up. Its synagogue rejected him after he read from Isaiah, and Nathanael asked whether anything good could come from it.
34337: Excavations under the Church of the Annunciation and the nearby Sisters of Nazareth convent show a modest early Roman village with houses cut partly into rock and kokhim tombs. The "Nazareth Inscription", a Roman edict against tomb violation, is of uncertain provenance.
34340: A fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee that became Jesus' base, "his own city". He taught in its synagogue, healed Peter's mother-in-law and a paralysed man lowered through a roof, yet rebuked the town for unbelief.
34341: The white limestone synagogue (4th to 5th century) stands on basalt foundations that may belong to the 1st-century synagogue. Nearby, a house venerated from the 1st century was enlarged into a house-church and later an octagonal church, identified by excavators as Peter's house.
34344: The hometown of Philip, Andrew and Peter, near where the five thousand were fed and a blind man was healed in stages. Philip the tetrarch raised it to a city named Julias. Two sites compete: et-Tell (shown), excavated since 1987, and el-Araj nearer the lakeshore.
34345: et-Tell has a substantial Iron Age city (probably Geshurite) but thin Roman remains. Excavations at el-Araj since 2016 found early Roman occupation and a Byzantine church that its excavators propose is the Church of the Apostles described by pilgrims.
34348: A town in the hills above Capernaum, condemned by Jesus with Bethsaida because it did not repent despite his mighty works.
34349: The ruins include a 3rd to 4th-century basalt synagogue with carved decoration and a stone chair inscribed in Aramaic, often compared to the "seat of Moses" in Matt 23:2.
34351: The village where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, his first sign in John, and the hometown of Nathanael. Many scholars favour Khirbet Qana (shown) on the north edge of the Beit Netofa valley; the traditional pilgrim site is Kafr Kanna near Nazareth.
34352: Excavations at Khirbet Qana found a 1st-century Jewish village and a cave complex venerated by Christians in the Byzantine and Crusader periods, consistent with medieval pilgrim descriptions.
34355: A village on the northern slope of the Hill of Moreh where Jesus met a funeral procession and raised the only son of a widow. The Arab village of Nein preserves the name.
34358: A prosperous fish-processing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, probably the hometown of Mary Magdalene. Greek sources call it Taricheae ("place of salting fish").
34359: Excavations since 2009 uncovered a 1st-century synagogue with the Magdala Stone, carved with a seven-branched menorah, along with a harbour, markets and ritual baths.
34363: A city at a spring of the Jordan beneath Mount Hermon, rebuilt by Philip the tetrarch and named for Caesar. In its region Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ and Jesus spoke of building his church.
34364: Beside the spring cave are niches and shrines to the god Pan and a temple to Augustus built by Herod the Great, as well as a later palace complex.
34367: A dome-shaped mountain rising from the Jezreel plain where Barak gathered his army against Sisera. Christian tradition from at least the 4th century identifies it as the mountain of the Transfiguration; many modern scholars prefer Mount Hermon, nearer Caesarea Philippi where the preceding episode is set.
34368: The summit holds Byzantine and Crusader church remains under the modern Franciscan Basilica of the Transfiguration (1924) and a Greek Orthodox monastery.
34371: The Samaritan town near Jacob's well and Joseph's tomb where Jesus spoke with the Samaritan woman about living water and true worship. It is commonly identified with the village of Askar, though some equate it with Shechem itself; the point shown is Jacob's Well.
34372: Jacob's Well (Bir Ya'qub), now within a Greek Orthodox church, has been venerated since at least the 4th century, when the Bordeaux Pilgrim described it.
34375: A village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus, where Jesus raised Lazarus and was anointed before his death. Distinct from "Bethany beyond the Jordan" where John baptised.
34376: A rock-cut tomb has been venerated as Lazarus' tomb since the 4th century; churches were built there from the Byzantine period onward.
34380: The village to which two disciples were walking when the risen Jesus joined them and was recognised in the breaking of bread. The site shown is Emmaus Nicopolis (Imwas), favoured by Eusebius and Jerome, though it lies about 160 stadia from Jerusalem, matching a minority manuscript reading rather than the usual 60; alternatives include el-Qubeibeh, Abu Ghosh and Motza (Roman Colonia), the last at roughly the right distance.
34381: Imwas has remains of a Byzantine basilica and baptistery. At Motza a Second Temple Jewish settlement has been excavated.
34383: A garden or olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives across the Kidron, where Jesus prayed in anguish and was arrested after Judas' kiss. The traditional site has been marked by churches since the 4th century.
34384: The Church of All Nations (1924) stands over remains of a 4th-century church and a Crusader church. A 2012 study dated the oldest olive trees in the garden to around the 12th century, and a ritual bath found in 2020 suggests 1st-century activity nearby.
34387: "The place of the skull", just outside Jerusalem's walls, where Jesus was crucified, with a garden tomb nearby. Most archaeologists accept the traditional site in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (shown); the Garden Tomb north of the Damascus Gate, proposed in the 19th century, remains popular with Protestant visitors but its tomb is generally dated to the Iron Age.
34388: The Holy Sepulchre site was a former quarry outside the city wall in Jesus' day, with 1st-century tombs nearby; Constantine's church was dedicated in 335. Restoration in 2016 exposed the original limestone burial bench. The heel bone of a crucified man named Jehohanan, with a nail still in it, was found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968.
34390: A league of Greek-style cities, mostly east of the Jordan, including Scythopolis, Gadara, Hippos, Pella, Gerasa and Philadelphia. The healed demoniac proclaimed Jesus there, and Jesus later passed through it healing a deaf man.
34391: Well-preserved Roman cities such as Jerash (Gerasa), Umm Qais (Gadara), Hippos (Sussita) and Beth-shean (Scythopolis) show the region's colonnaded streets, theatres and temples.
34393: The city Herod Antipas founded around AD 20 on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee and named for the emperor Tiberius; it became his capital. The Gospels do not record Jesus entering it. Later it became a leading centre of rabbinic learning where the Mishnah and Jerusalem Talmud were finalised.
34394: Remains include a Roman theatre, a monumental gate, and the Hammat Tiberias synagogue with its zodiac mosaic (4th century).
34398: Herod the Great's harbour city and the seat of Roman governors of Judea. Peter baptised the centurion Cornelius here, Herod Agrippa I died here, and Paul was held for two years before appealing to Caesar.
34399: The Pilate Stone (found 1961) names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea. Herod's artificial harbour Sebastos, built with hydraulic concrete, a theatre, hippodrome and seaside palace survive.
34403: A town on the coastal plain near Joppa where Peter healed the paralysed Aeneas. Renamed Diospolis, it hosted the synod of 415 at which Pelagius was acquitted.
34404: A large Roman floor mosaic of animals and ships was uncovered in Lod in 1996.
34407: Capital of Roman Syria and one of the empire's largest cities. Believers were first called Christians here; its church sent out Paul and Barnabas, and Paul confronted Peter here over table fellowship with Gentiles. Ignatius was later its bishop.
34408: Excavations (1932-1939) recovered many fine Roman mosaics now in the Hatay museum. The cave church of St Peter on Mount Staurin is traditional. The 2023 earthquake severely damaged the old city.
34410: The chief city of Cilicia on the Cydnus river, noted for its schools, and the birthplace of Paul, who called it "no mean city". Paul returned here after his conversion until Barnabas fetched him to Antioch.
34411: A section of Roman street with basalt paving has been uncovered; the much-visited "St Paul's Well" is traditional only.
34413: The large island off the Syrian coast, Barnabas' homeland and the first stop of his and Paul's mission, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed. Barnabas later returned there with John Mark.
34415: The main port on the east coast of Cyprus, where Barnabas and Saul first preached in the Jewish synagogues on their first journey. Later tradition holds that Barnabas was martyred and buried near here.
34416: Ruins include a Roman gymnasium, theatre and baths, and the large 4th-century basilica of Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis.
34418: The Roman capital of Cyprus on the west coast, where Paul blinded the sorcerer Bar-Jesus (Elymas) and the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed. From here Acts begins calling Saul by the name Paul.
34419: Nea Paphos has extensive Roman villas with mosaics, now a UNESCO site. Inscriptions mentioning a Sergius Paulus exist, though their link to Acts' proconsul is debated.
34421: A city of Pamphylia where John Mark left Paul and Barnabas to return to Jerusalem. On the way back the missionaries preached there before sailing from Attalia.
34422: Perga's ruins include Hellenistic gate towers, a colonnaded street with a water channel, a theatre and a large stadium.
34425: A Roman colony near modern Yalvac where Paul preached his longest recorded synagogue sermon and then announced a turn to the Gentiles after opposition. Paul and Barnabas returned through it to strengthen the disciples.
34426: Remains include an imperial temple to Augustus, an aqueduct and a 4th-century church. Fragments of Augustus' Res Gestae were found here.
34429: A city of Lycaonia where Paul and Barnabas preached with signs until a plot to stone them forced them to flee. The 2nd-century *Acts of Paul and Thecla* sets Thecla's story here.
34431: A Roman colony in Lycaonia where Paul healed a lame man, the crowds hailed him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus, and Paul was then stoned and left for dead. It was Timothy's home.
34432: An inscription naming the colony was found at Zoldera (Klistra), near Hatunsaray, by J. R. S. Sterrett in 1885, establishing the location; the mound is largely unexcavated.
34434: The easternmost city reached on Paul's first journey, where many became disciples; Gaius of Derbe later travelled with Paul. It is usually identified with Kerti Huyuk; Devri Sehri nearby is a less favoured alternative.
34435: Inscriptions found in 1956 and 1962 naming Derbe (including a bishop of Derbe) led to the Kerti Huyuk identification.
34437: A Roman colony and port on the Aegean near ancient Troy. Paul saw the vision of the man of Macedonia here, and on a later visit Eutychus fell from a window during Paul's long talk and was restored. Paul left his cloak and parchments here.
34439: A Roman colony on the Via Egnatia, the first city in Europe where Paul founded a church. Lydia was baptised by the river, Paul and Silas were beaten and jailed and the jailer believed, and the church later supported Paul and received his letter to the Philippians.
34440: The UNESCO-listed site has the Roman forum, a theatre, several early Christian basilicas, and a crypt traditionally called Paul's prison.
34442: Capital of the province of Macedonia on the Via Egnatia. Paul's preaching won converts but provoked a riot, and he left after a short stay, later writing two letters to the young church.
34443: An inscription from the Vardar Gate uses the title "politarchs" for city officials, the same uncommon term Luke uses in Acts 17:6. The Roman forum and Galerius' palace complex survive.
34446: A Macedonian town where the Jews were "more noble" than those in Thessalonica because they examined the scriptures daily to test Paul's message. Sopater of Berea later travelled with Paul.
34447: The intellectual centre of the Greek world, where Paul reasoned in the synagogue and marketplace and addressed the Areopagus about the "unknown god". A few believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris.
34448: The Agora, the Areopagus hill below the Acropolis, and numerous altars and temples illustrate Luke's description of a city "full of idols".
34450: A wealthy Roman colony on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese and capital of Achaia. Paul stayed eighteen months working with Priscilla and Aquila; the church he founded received at least two of his letters.
34451: The Gallio inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's proconsulship to about AD 51-52, anchoring Paul's chronology. Corinth has the judgement platform (bema), the temple of Apollo and a pavement inscription naming an Erastus as aedile, possibly the city official of Rom 16:23.
34454: Corinth's eastern port on the Saronic Gulf, where Paul cut his hair because of a vow. Phoebe, the deacon who probably carried Paul's letter to Rome, served the church here.
34455: Underwater and shoreline remains include harbour moles, warehouses and an early Christian basilica.
34457: Capital of the province of Asia and home of the great temple of Artemis. Paul spent over two years here, the silversmiths rioted in the theatre, and it is the first of the seven churches in Revelation. Tradition links the apostle John with Ephesus, and the Council of Ephesus met here in 431.
34458: Excavations reveal the theatre (seating about 24,000), the Library of Celsus, terrace houses, and the foundations of the Artemision, one of the seven wonders. The Basilica of St John stands at Selcuk.
34460: An Ionian port south of Ephesus where Paul summoned the Ephesian elders and gave his farewell address. Paul later left Trophimus sick here.
